lead: Every load on a machine part changes with time in its own way. It may be steady, it may repeat or reverse thousands of times, or it may arrive as a sudden blow. The time history decides the analysis: a static stress check for a steady load, a fatigue check for a repeated one, and an energy balance for an impact. This chapter sorts loads into the three kinds and shows why a load applied suddenly doubles the stress, while a weight dropped from a small height can multiply it hundreds of times.
prereq: You need σ = P/A and δ = PL/(AE) from direct stresses.

items: Static load: its size and direction stay constant, or change so slowly that inertia is negligible. A water tank on a roof, a lift hanging at rest on its rope.

Dynamic (variable) load: its size or direction changes with time, often in a repeating cycle. A gear tooth loaded once per turn, a connecting rod pushed and pulled every stroke, a rotating shaft whose bending stress reverses each revolution. Repeated stress causes fatigue: see failure theories and fatigue design.
Impact (shock) load: a large force for a very short time, usually because one body strikes another. A hammer blow, a railway buffer, a car wheel hitting a pothole, a rope catching a falling load.

blocks.text: The same part may see all three. A crane hook carries a static load while the load hangs still, a dynamic load while the crane travels, and an impact when a slack rope suddenly takes the load. Figure 1.5.1 draws the three histories side by side.

sections.h3: Suddenly applied load: twice the stress

blocks.text: Hang a weight W on a bar gradually, so that the force grows from 0 to W. The work done, ½Wδ, is stored as strain energy and the stress is σ = W/A, where A is the area of the bar.

Now let the same weight act suddenly at full value with no drop (it is held just touching the collar and released). The weight does work Wδ<sub>max</sub> as the bar stretches, but the bar stores only ½P<sub>max</sub>δ<sub>max</sub>, where P<sub>max</sub> is the largest force in the bar. Equating, P<sub>max</sub> = 2W, so σ<sub>max</sub> = 2W/A. A suddenly applied load gives twice the stress and twice the extension of the same load applied gradually; the bar then oscillates about the static position.

Let W fall through a height h onto a collar at the end of a bar of length L, area A and modulus E. At the lowest point the weight has lost potential energy W(h + δ<sub>max</sub>), and the bar stores σ<sub>max</sub>²AL/(2E). With δ<sub>max</sub> = σ<sub>max</sub>L/E, the energy balance is a quadratic in σ<sub>max</sub> whose positive root gives the impact factor.

k is the impact factor (no unit); σ<sub>st</sub> = W/A is the static stress and δ<sub>st</sub> = WL/(AE) the static extension, both for the weight applied gradually; h is the height of fall (same unit as δ<sub>st</sub>). For h = 0, k = 2, the sudden-load result. When h is much larger than δ<sub>st</sub>, k ≈ √(2h/δ<sub>st</sub>), and then σ<sub>max</sub> ≈ √(2EWh/(AL)).

items: Convert everything to N and mm (stress in MPa).
Find σ<sub>st</sub> = W/A and δ<sub>st</sub> = WL/(AE).
Find k = 1 + √(1 + 2h/δ<sub>st</sub>), then σ<sub>max</sub> = kσ<sub>st</sub> and δ<sub>max</sub> = kδ<sub>st</sub>.
Check the energy: W(h + δ<sub>max</sub>) should equal σ<sub>max</sub>²AL/(2E).

blocks.text: The last formula shows two surprises. A longer bar lowers the impact stress, because it stores the same energy at a lower stress, and a larger area lowers it only as 1/√A, not 1/A: what counts is the volume AL that works at full stress. That is why a bolt that takes shock has its shank turned down to the root diameter of the thread: the whole length then works at the same stress and stores more energy before the threads reach their limit. Impact design with springs and energy absorbers continues in the chapter on impact and shock loading.

examples.question: A 10 kg weight falls 100 mm onto a collar at the lower end of a vertical steel bar 1 m long, 500 mm² in area, E = 200 GPa. Find the maximum stress and extension, and compare them with the gradually and suddenly applied cases. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
steps: Data in N and mm: W = 10 × 9.81 = 98.1 N; h = 100 mm; L = 1000 mm; A = 500 mm²; E = 200,000 N/mm².
Static stress: σ<sub>st</sub> = 98.1/500 = 0.196 MPa. Static extension: δ<sub>st</sub> = 98.1 × 1000/(500 × 200,000) = 9.81 × 10⁻⁴ mm.
Maximum stress σ<sub>max</sub> = 452.5 × 0.196 = 88.8 MPa. Maximum extension δ<sub>max</sub> = 452.5 × 9.81 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.444 mm.
Energy check: W(h + δ<sub>max</sub>) = 98.1 × 100.444 = 9854 N·mm; σ<sub>max</sub>²AL/(2E) = 88.79² × 500 × 1000/400,000 = 9855 N·mm. They agree to rounding.
Gradual load: 0.196 MPa. Sudden load (h = 0): 2 × 0.196 = 0.392 MPa.
examples.answer: σ<sub>max</sub> = 88.8 MPa and δ<sub>max</sub> = 0.444 mm; that is 452 times the gradual stress of 0.196 MPa and 226 times the sudden-load stress of 0.392 MPa.

examples.question: For the same bar and weight, from what height may the weight fall if the stress must not exceed 160 MPa?
steps: Allowed impact factor: k = 160/0.196 = 815.5 (using σ<sub>st</sub> = 0.1962 MPa).
examples.answer: The weight may fall at most about 325 mm.

traps: Treating a suddenly applied load as a falling one. Sudden load with no drop gives k = 2; any drop height gives more.
Leaving out δ<sub>max</sub> in the lost potential energy W(h + δ<sub>max</sub>). It matters when h is small.
Mixing units: h in mm with δ<sub>st</sub> in m, or E in GPa with areas in mm². Work in N and mm throughout.
Expecting a bigger bar to halve the impact stress. Doubling A cuts it only by about √2, and a longer bar helps.
Calling a vibrating but steady-amplitude load "static". If the stress repeats, fatigue must be checked.

quiz.q: Define static, dynamic and impact loads, with one example each.
quiz.a: Static: constant in size and direction (a roof tank). Dynamic: varies with time, often cyclically (a gear tooth). Impact: a large force for a very short time (a hammer blow).

quiz.q: Why does a suddenly applied load give twice the stress of a gradual one?
quiz.a: The suddenly applied weight does work Wδ while the bar stores only ½P<sub>max</sub>δ; equating gives P<sub>max</sub> = 2W, so σ = 2W/A.

quiz.q: Why classify the load by time before choosing the analysis?
quiz.a: The time history decides the failure mode: a steady load needs a static stress check, a repeated load a fatigue check, a sudden one an energy or impact-factor calculation.

quiz.q: A 2 kN load is applied suddenly to a bar of area 100 mm². Find the maximum stress.
quiz.a: σ<sub>st</sub> = 2000/100 = 20 MPa; sudden load gives 2 × 20 = 40 MPa.

quiz.q: A weight gives a static extension of 0.50 mm and falls through 50 mm. Find the impact factor.
A designer doubles the area of a bar to halve its impact stress. Does it work?
quiz.a: No. For a large drop σ<sub>max</sub> ≈ √(2EWh/(AL)), which falls only as 1/√A: doubling A reduces the stress to 1/√2 = 0.71 of its value. Lengthening the bar also helps.

quiz.q: A crane lifts a load, the load slips and the rope catches it. Which kinds of load act?
quiz.a: Static while the load hangs, dynamic while the crane moves, and impact when the slack rope catches the falling load.

beyond: Industry checks impact with drop tests, cushioning design and explicit finite element analysis that follows the stress waves through the part. Shock response spectra compare a measured pulse with what a product can survive, and strain-rate effects raise the strength of steel in crash events. Search next for drop testing, shock response spectrum and explicit dynamics.

figure.caption: The three load histories, sketched (not to scale). A static load stays put, a dynamic load repeats and calls for a fatigue check, and an impact is a short, high spike: in the worked example a 10 kg weight dropped 100 mm raises the stress from 0.196 MPa to 88.8 MPa.
